prize_parts.citation: for pioneering the construction of cubic-kilometre neutrino telescopes and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: IceCube is the clearest example on the list of a new instrument opening a new observational window. A cubic-kilometre of Antarctic ice was instrumented, and it delivered a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos well above atmospheric backgrounds, a first compelling source association (TXS 0506+056, 2017-2018), evidence from NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane, and a direct handle on where cosmic rays are accelerated. The result is built on patient work in calibration of the ice, background rejection and blind analysis, which is the kind of systematics-limited effort that makes a result credible. The diffuse flux has been seen in several channels inside IceCube and is supported by other telescopes (Baikal-GVD, ANTARES), so this is not a single-experiment claim. I now put Spiering in the third place because the AMANDA/Baikal/DUMAND lineage is what made a large neutrino telescope a believable proposition, and Halzen and Karle alone would leave that history out. Three names (Halzen as conceiver and leader, Karle as the builder of the detector and the early analyses, Spiering as the pioneer who carried the idea across the Baikal and AMANDA/IceCube programmes) is a defensible, compact allocation. No neutrino-astronomy prize has been given before, so the field is not recycled.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and maturity together. A very large collaboration made the discovery, the founding concepts go back to Markov and Zheleznykh and to DUMAND, and any three names leave out people with a real claim (for example Baikal and AMANDA leaders, or those who led the 2013 and 2018 analyses). Source-level evidence is still at modest significance for individual objects, and KM3NeT has not yet delivered an independent confirmation of source associations at IceCube's depth. If colleagues judge that the diffuse flux alone is a discovery of an astrophysical component but not yet of astrophysical sources, a prize now could be read as slightly early for the astrophysical interpretation, even though the detection itself is secure.

responses.point: Ulf ranks the experimental Higgs discovery first as the largest unrecognised discovery in the field, with Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee as a workable three-person set across ATLAS and CMS, while admitting that Della Negra is excluded at real cost.
responses.response: I agree on the physics and I ranked B019 second myself, so this is not a disagreement about merit. My difficulty is the attribution, and I think it is more serious than a cost of exclusion. Two independent collaborations of thousands made the discovery, and a set of founding spokespersons and one announcement-time spokesperson is a statement about leadership roles rather than about who made the decisive scientific contribution. Choosing Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee also drops Della Negra, who is as senior a founder as Virdee. For IceCube the credit chain from Halzen through Karle to Spiering is shorter and each person has an identifiable decisive role. I would keep B019 as the main alternative and would want the committee to say in advance how it would justify the three names before we adopt it.

responses.point: Stefan places optical lattice clocks first: a new measurement technique, 1e-18 uncertainties, independent confirmation in several laboratories, and a clean two-name credit for Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I take the credit argument seriously, because Katori and Ye is the cleanest attribution on the whole shortlist, and I ranked B059 fifth. As an instrument builder I value the technique. My qualification is that I am not the right person to judge whether the lattice clock is a distinct discovery or an extension of the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems, and you and Eva Lindroth are better placed to say that. Where I differ is on what is more novel. A clock at 1e-18 is a large improvement of an existing observable, while neutrino astronomy opens a channel that did not exist. I also note that the redefinition of the second is still pending, which suggests that a clock prize would be as sound in a later year. If you can show that the committee's own precedent treats this as a new discovery, I would move B059 higher.

responses.point: Goran ranks circuit QED first as the architecture behind superconducting processors, with Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf as a theory-plus-experiment trio, and he flags the overlap with the 2025 prize and defers on his own conflict.
responses.response: I respect that the physics is mature, and the experimental result of strong coupling on a chip is real. My concern is the one you raise yourself. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is only a year old, and I would find it hard to justify a second superconducting-circuit prize so quickly without a clear separation of what is new. Girvin and Devoret are also outside the credited names, and I suspect much of the practical impact comes from device engineering such as the transmon rather than from circuit QED as a concept. Since you have declared that you work in this area, I would ask that you do not lead the committee's judgement on credit in B013, and I will ask outside reviewers to look at that point if it goes forward. I do not find it in my top group.

responses.point: Olle ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first: a quantitative theoretical prediction of flat bands followed by a decisive experimental demonstration of correlated insulators and superconductivity, with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero.
responses.response: I see why the prediction followed by confirmation is attractive, and I accept that it has been reproduced by many groups. I disagree about timing. It is about eight years old and the origin of the superconductivity is still debated, and Eva Lindroth, Bernhard Mehlig and Ulf Danielsson have all raised sample dependence or premature recognition. You note yourself that Yuan Cao and other first-author experimentalists are outside the credited list, which makes the fairness question a live one. In a condensed-matter case I rely on you and the others, so I would ask whether the committee would be comfortable waiting five more years for the pairing mechanism to settle before awarding it, and whether there is an argument that the discovery of the correlated phases is secure enough without that.

uncertainties: Whether Spiering or another pioneer (Baikal or AMANDA leaders, Markov and Zheleznykh lineage) should be the third name, and whether credit for the decisive 2013 evidence and 2018 source results lies with other collaboration leaders.

Whether individual source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane) are strong enough, and independently confirmed enough by KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD, to treat the prize as mature for the astrophysical interpretation.
How the committee will resolve attribution in B019 if it proves the preferred choice of colleagues, because I cannot see a defensible three-name set there.
Whether optical lattice clocks count as a distinct discovery relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which is outside my expertise and needs the atomic-physics members or outside reviewers.
I have not independently verified the collaboration history in the opening arguments, which comes from memory.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I work in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur, not IceCube, and I know of no institutional link between KTH and any credited name for B043. I do share a field, astroparticle physics, with the IceCube community, and I flag that proximity so that colleagues can weigh my judgement of this candidate accordingly.
